Counsel for the complainant: Sh. Himanshu Nagpal Ld. Counsel for the Accused: Sh. Naresh Kumar JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Rajinder Kumar Jain HUF represented by its Karta Sh. Rajinder Kumar Jain (hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant") against Jeffrey Exports Pvt. Ltd. through its directors (hereinafter referred to as "the Accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, accused had placed an order to the complainant for supply of export quality fabrics and accordingly the transaction took place between both the parties at Delhi. That, frequent business transactions took place between the complainant and the accused in accordance to which the complainant used to supply the export quality fabrics and in order to receive payments from the accused, the complainant used to raise invoices against which the accused used to make payment through cheques/cash. The details of the invoices are on record. That, after supplying the goods to the accused, the complainant requested the accused to make the payments for the goods supplied, so in discharge of his CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 3 of 11 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:29 +0530 liability the accused issued a cheque bearing no. 652396 dated 03.05.2015 amounting to Rs. 1,90,645/- drawn on Indian Bank, Defence Colony, New Delhi-110024 and that the accused had ensured the complainant that the said cheque will be encashed on its presentation. B. That, believing the assurances and representations of the accused to be true and correct, the complainant presented the aforesaid cheque for realization with his bank Citi Bank, New Delhi. That, the cheque got dishonoured upon presentation with the endorsement "Payment Stopped by Drawer" vide cheque return memo dated 09.06.2015. C. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 06.07.2015, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and wilfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the Authorised representative of the complainant examined himself as CW-1 on affidavit being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record Invoice Ex. CW1/1; Cheque in question Ex. CW1/2; Return memo Ex. CW1/3; Legal demand notice Ex. CW1/4; Original Postal receipt Ex. CW1/5 and Ex. CW1/6. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 4 of 11 AASTHA SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:34 +0530 5. Upon the appearance of the accused through its director Sh. Anil Bagga, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 09.05.2019 to which he pleaded not guilty. At this stage, the accused through its AR/Director Anil Bagga stated that he has not signed the cheques and he does not know how the complainant got into the possession of the cheques in question and no material as alleged by the complainant was sent to him. The accused through its AR/Director Anil Bagga has further stated that the copy of the bills were not addressed to him. He has further denied receiving the legal demand notice. 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Vide separate statement of Ld. Counsel for the accused dated 13.02.2025, CE was closed. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 03.06.2025 wherein the accused through its AR/ Director Deepak Bagga stated that he does not wish to lead DE. Therefore the right of the accused to lead DE was closed by this court vide order dated 03.06.2025. 8. Final arguments heard on behalf of both the parties. Record perused and considered. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 5 of 11 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:39 +0530 IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 6 of 11 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:44 +0530 IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 652377 dated 05.05.2015 for Rs. 4,31,172/- drawn on Citi Bank, Defence Colony, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/2). It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused company and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memo dated 09.06.2015 (Ex. CW1/3) due to the reason "Drawer Signature Differs." By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 07.07.2015 (Ex. CW1/4) was dispatched on 07.07.2015 vide Courier and Speed Post (Ex. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 7 of 11 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:52 +0530 CW1/5 & Ex. CW1/6), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheque in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has denied the receipt of legal demand notice. However, the AR of accused company in the statement of the accused has admitted that the address on record is the correct address of the accused company. Furthermore, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 8 of 11 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:31:57 +0530 The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 9 of 11 AASTHA SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:32:04 +0530 18. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. Ld. Counsel for the accused in his legal notice u/s 251 CrPC has stated that he does not know how the complainant got into the possession of the cheques and that they never received the goods as mentioned by the complainant in the invoice placed on record Ex. CW1/1. The accused director in his legal notice u/s 251 CrPC has stated that the copy of the bills was never addressed to him as well. 19. It is to be noted that accused no. 1 company Jeffrey Exports Pvt. Ltd. has been made the accused in the present matter, through its directors. The cheque has been drawn on the account of the accused no. 1 company and is signed by the authorized signatory of the accused no. 1 company Sh. Deepak Bagga, who was also substituted as the AR of the accused no. 1 company vide order dated 03.06.2025. Furthermore, the accused company was always represented by a representative as the notice u/s 251 CrPC was framed against the accused no. 1 company through its directors Anil Bagga and Rita Bagga and the statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC was recorded by Sh. Deepak Bagga, as AR on behalf of the accused no. 1 company. Therefore the accused no. 1 company had an opportunity to rebut the presumption u/s 139 read with Section 118 , NI Act. 20. The accused has made mere bald assertions at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC and at the stage of Section 313 CrPC that the bills were never addressed to the accused or the material mentioned on the bill was never delivered to the accused, but he has not brought any oral or documentary evidence to substantiate his claim. Furthermore, he has nowhere justified how the cheques got into the possession of the complainant. No complaint has also been filed on behalf of the accused qua the misuse of said cheques by the complainant, which creates a doubt as to the credibility of the version of the accused. CC No. 2298/2015 624440/2016 RAJINDER KUMAR JAIN Vs. JEFFREY EXPORTS PVT LTD page 10 of 11 AASTHA SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2025.09.23 15:32:10 +0530 21. It is also a settled law that the statements made by the accused in reply to notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. or in his examination under Section 281 read with Section 313 Cr.P.C. are not on oath and hence are not substantive pieces of evidence. At best, they may be an explanation of the incriminating circumstances against the accused but are devoid of any presumption as to their truthfulness. Support is drawn from the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi cited as V.S. Yadav Vs. Reena ; 172 (2010) DLT 561. The entire defence of the accused is nothing but a set of bald assertions unsubstantiated by any cogent or reliable evidence. His oral assertions at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC, Section 313 CrPC stand rebutted by documentary evidence brought forth on behalf of the complainant. Thus, there is nothing available on record for the court to believe that the defence plea disclosed by the accused in his reply to the notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C or Section 313 CrPC is plausible. 22. In the present case, the accused has failed to even create any doubt, let alone discharging his burden of proof to rebut the presumption u/s 138 , NI Act. The accused has neither brought any witness nor any documentary evidence on record to substantiate his claim. It is the duty of the accused to punch holes in the story of the complainant which he has not been able to do. On the other hand, the complainant has brought documentary evidence to prove his version of the story alongwith the benefit of presumption u/s 139 , NI Act in his favour. 23. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has been fulfilled in the present case. 24. Accordingly, Accused no. 1 company Jeffrey Exports Pvt. Ltd. through its directors is held guilty and is convicted of the offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 25. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost as per rules.
